dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: How did the event go?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: By and large, pretty well.

cards.expression: In the grand scheme of things
cards.usageNote: Minimizes a detail compared with what matters overall.
examples: In the grand scheme of things, one missed train isn't much.
That delay was small in the grand scheme of things.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: I keep thinking about the typo.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In the grand scheme of things, it doesn't matter.

cards.usageNote: Says something happens in most cases, though not always.
examples: More often than not, the bus arrives late.
More often than not, she walks to work.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Does the café get crowded?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: More often than not, yes.

cards.usageNote: Describes a situation that is generally true with exceptions.
examples: For the most part, the instructions were clear.
The city is safe for the most part.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did the new routine help?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: For the most part, yes.

cards.usageNote: Limits how far a statement or agreement applies.
examples: To a certain extent, I agree with that criticism.
Prices depend on location to a certain extent.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Does experience matter more than training?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: To a certain extent.

cards.usageNote: Adds an important supporting point to an argument.
examples: The place is noisy, not to mention expensive.
It saves time, not to mention money.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why don't you like the hotel?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: It's far away, not to mention overpriced.

cards.usageNote: Emphasizes that a harder thing is even less likely than an easier one.
examples: I barely have time to cook, let alone bake.
She can't afford a bike, let alone a car.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can we finish two reports tonight?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We can't finish one, let alone two.

cards.usageNote: Emphasizes something that is assumed to be obvious.
examples: Safety comes first; that goes without saying.
That goes without saying, but it's worth repeating.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: We should tell the truth, right?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: That goes without saying.

cards.usageNote: Says behavior or an event reveals a great deal without words.
examples: It speaks volumes that she stayed to help.
That silence speaks volumes about their priorities.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: He showed up even though he was sick.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: That speaks volumes.

cards.usageNote: Points to a detail as revealing something important.
examples: The fact that nobody replied is telling.
It's telling that the complaints keep coming.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: They refused to share the numbers.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: That's telling.

cards.tr: Şundan emin olun / sakın yanlış anlamayın
cards.usageNote: Firmly emphasizes a point that should not be underestimated.
examples: Make no mistake, this will take real effort.
Make no mistake: we still have work to do.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Does a small team mean an easy launch?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Make no mistake, it doesn't.

cards.usageNote: Humorously signals strong feelings or complaints about a subject.
examples: Don't get me started on airline fees.
The parking situation? Don't get me started.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: How was dealing with customer support?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Don't get me started.

cards.usageNote: Introduces an unsurprising or obvious outcome.
examples: Needless to say, everyone was disappointed.
Needless to say, we double-checked the address.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did everyone leave when the alarm sounded?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Needless to say, we all did.

cards.usageNote: Introduces what you would do if a difficult situation becomes urgent.
examples: If push comes to shove, we can take the train.
I can work on Sunday if push comes to shove.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What if the hotel cancels?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: If push comes to shove, we'll find another.

cards.expression: When it comes down to it
cards.usageNote: Introduces what matters when a decision must finally be made.
examples: When it comes down to it, I trust her judgment.
When it comes down to it, comfort matters most.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Would you take a lower salary?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: When it comes down to it, it depends on the role.

cards.expression: We may have to bite the bullet
cards.tr: Dişimizi sıkıp zor bir şeye katlanmamız gerekebilir
cards.usageNote: Suggests accepting an unpleasant but necessary action.
examples: We may have to bite the bullet and pay for repairs.
I bit the bullet and made the difficult call.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What if the cheaper option fails?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We may have to bite the bullet.

cards.usageNote: Says a complex problem has no easy universal solution.
examples: There's no silver bullet for learning a language.
Better software helps, but there's no silver bullet.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can one tool fix everything?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: There's no silver bullet.

cards.expression: We're not out of the woods yet
cards.usageNote: Warns that difficulties remain despite some progress.
examples: The fever is lower, but we're not out of the woods yet.
Sales improved, though we're not out of the woods yet.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is the problem finally over?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We're not out of the woods yet.

cards.usageNote: Describes a situation requiring careful balance to avoid trouble.
examples: We're walking a fine line between helpful and intrusive.
The team is walking a fine line on costs.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can we shorten the review without risk?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We're walking a fine line.

cards.usageNote: Warns that an action may produce the opposite of the intended result.
examples: A public complaint could backfire.
Trying to rush them might backfire.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Should we surprise her with the news?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: That could backfire.

cards.usageNote: Warns that a decision may influence future similar cases.
examples: An exception here might set a precedent.
That decision could set a precedent for future requests.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why not waive the fee just once?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: It might set a precedent.

cards.expression: Let's not open that can of worms
cards.usageNote: Suggests avoiding a topic likely to create further complications.
examples: Let's not open that can of worms tonight.
Changing every rule now would open a can of worms.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Should we revisit the whole agreement?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Let's not open that can of worms.

cards.usageNote: Describes something with significant advantages and disadvantages.
examples: Remote work is a double-edged sword for some people.
More choice can be a double-edged sword.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is instant messaging always helpful?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: It's a double-edged sword.

cards.usageNote: Says two or more people face a similar difficulty.
examples: We're in the same boat with these deadlines.
Everyone is in the same boat this week.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: I'm struggling to keep up.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We're in the same boat.

cards.expression: The ball is in your court
cards.usageNote: Means the next decision or action belongs to someone else.
examples: I've sent the details; the ball is in your court.
We made our offer, so the ball is in their court.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What happens after I get the quote?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The ball is in your court.

cards.expression: Let's not get ahead of ourselves
cards.usageNote: Warns against planning as if an uncertain outcome is guaranteed.
examples: Let's not get ahead of ourselves before the approval.
We haven't signed yet; let's not get ahead of ourselves.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Should we announce the move?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Let's not get ahead of ourselves.

cards.expression: I don't want to jinx it
cards.usageNote: Says you hesitate to celebrate or predict success too soon.
examples: The interviews went well, but I don't want to jinx it.
I think we'll win; I just don't want to jinx it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is the project finally on schedule?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: So far, but I don't want to jinx it.

cards.usageNote: Says a long task is nearly complete.
examples: We're on the home stretch with the renovation.
One more review and we're on the home stretch.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: How much work is left?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We're on the home stretch.

cards.expression: It's been a long time coming
cards.usageNote: Says something has taken a long time to happen.
examples: This promotion has been a long time coming.
The station renovation was a long time coming.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: You finally got the keys?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Yes, it's been a long time coming.

cards.usageNote: Describes an apparent problem that later brings benefits.
examples: Losing the apartment feels awful now, but it's a blessing in disguise.
Losing the first apartment was a blessing in disguise.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: You actually liked changing jobs?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: It was a blessing in disguise.

cards.usageNote: Names a final event that ends someone's patience.
examples: Another canceled meeting? That's the last straw.
When the bill doubled, it was the last straw.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did you leave the service?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: That was the last straw.

cards.usageNote: Expresses frustration after trying everything without success.
examples: I've tried everything and I'm at my wit's end.
I'm at my wit's end with this leak.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Have you fixed the connection yet?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: No, I'm at my wit's end.

cards.expression: I'll cross that bridge when I come to it
cards.usageNote: Defers worrying about a possible future problem until it actually occurs.
examples: I'll cross that bridge when I come to it.
If the rules change, I'll cross that bridge then.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What if you need to move again?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I'll cross that bridge when I come to it.

cards.usageNote: Introduces a contrast or a result that remains true despite an obstacle.
examples: Even though it was raining, we went for a walk.
She went to class even though she felt tired.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did the rain stop your walk?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Even though it was raining, we went for a walk.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: You can stay as long as you need.
As long as we leave early, we'll catch the train.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can I stay a little longer?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You can stay as long as you need.

cards.usageNote: Explains a reason, cause or justification for an action or conclusion.
examples: The game was canceled because of the rain.
Because of traffic, we arrived late.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why was the game canceled?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The game was canceled because of the rain.

cards.usageNote: Explains a reason, cause or justification for an action or conclusion.
examples: Thanks to your directions, I found the place.
We finished early thanks to everyone's help.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: How did you find the restaurant?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Thanks to your directions, I found the place.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: Let's take the bus instead of driving.
She ordered tea instead of coffee.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Are we going by car?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Let's take the bus instead of driving.

cards.usageNote: Introduces a contrast or a result that remains true despite an obstacle.
examples: I'll go even if nobody else comes.
Even if it takes longer, we should do it properly.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Will you still attend alone?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I'll go even if nobody else comes.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: We won't leave unless everyone is ready.
Unless it rains, we'll have lunch outside.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Are we eating outside tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We won't leave unless everyone is ready.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
I saved the receipt in case we need it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why are you carrying an umbrella?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

cards.usageNote: Links evidence or an action to its outcome, consequence or purpose.
examples: The roads were icy; as a result, school closed.
He practiced daily; as a result, he improved.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did the school close?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The roads were icy; as a result, school closed.

cards.usageNote: Adds a concrete illustration or highlights a specific example.
examples: Some cities, for example Boston, have cold winters.
You could try a new hobby, for example painting.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What kind of hobby do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Some cities, for example Boston, have cold winters.

cards.usageNote: Adds a related idea, comparison or simultaneous event.
examples: In addition to English, she studies Spanish.
We bought bread in addition to milk.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What else does she study?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In addition to English, she studies Spanish.

cards.usageNote: Places actions or ideas in a clear time or presentation order.
examples: At first, I didn't understand the instructions.
The task seemed easy at first.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did you understand the task immediately?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: At first, I didn't understand the instructions.

cards.usageNote: Places actions or ideas in a clear time or presentation order.
examples: We had dinner, and after that we watched a movie.
Finish your homework; after that, you can relax.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What did you do after dinner?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We had dinner, and after that we watched a movie.

cards.usageNote: Places actions or ideas in a clear time or presentation order.
examples: By the time I arrived, the meeting had started.
We'll be home by the time it gets dark.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did you arrive before the meeting started?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: By the time I arrived, the meeting had started.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: As usual, the bus was five minutes late.
She went for a run as usual.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Was the bus on time today?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: As usual, the bus was five minutes late.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: Leave now; otherwise, you'll miss the train.
Save your work, otherwise you may lose it.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why should I leave so early?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Leave now; otherwise, you'll miss the train.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: I thought the shop was closed; in fact, it was open.
In fact, we've met once before.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Was the shop really closed?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I thought the shop was closed; in fact, it was open.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: In the end, we chose the smaller apartment.
We argued for a while but agreed in the end.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which apartment did you choose?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In the end, we chose the smaller apartment.

cards.usageNote: Adds a related idea, comparison or simultaneous event.
examples: I like the job, but at the same time it's stressful.
She works and studies at the same time.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Do you enjoy your new job?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I like the job, but at the same time it's stressful.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: I'll support you no matter what happens.
No matter what the weather is like, we'll go.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Will you support my decision?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I'll support you no matter what happens.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: The north is dry; in contrast, the south gets heavy rain.
Her first book was serious; in contrast, this one is funny.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Do the two regions get similar rainfall?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The north is dry; in contrast, the south gets heavy rain.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: The rent is cheap; on the other hand, the commute is long.
The plan is quick; on the other hand, it costs more.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is the new apartment a good choice?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The rent is cheap; on the other hand, the commute is long.

cards.usageNote: Links evidence or an action to its outcome, consequence or purpose.
examples: The river flooded; as a consequence, roads were closed.
Demand fell; as a consequence, production slowed.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why are the roads closed?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The river flooded; as a consequence, roads were closed.

cards.usageNote: Introduces a contrast or a result that remains true despite an obstacle.
examples: Despite the delay, we arrived before noon.
She kept smiling despite the bad news.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did the delay ruin the trip?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Despite the delay, we arrived before noon.

cards.usageNote: Introduces a contrast or a result that remains true despite an obstacle.
examples: In spite of the noise, I fell asleep.
They finished the race in spite of the heat.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Could you sleep with all that noise?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In spite of the noise, I fell asleep.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: You can borrow the bike provided that you return it tonight.
The offer applies provided that you register first.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can I borrow your bike?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You can borrow the bike provided that you return it tonight.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: I wrote it down so that I wouldn't forget.
Speak clearly so that everyone can understand.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did you write that note?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I wrote it down so that I wouldn't forget.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: We left early in order to avoid traffic.
She took a course in order to improve her skills.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did you leave so early?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We left early in order to avoid traffic.

cards.usageNote: Adds a concrete illustration or highlights a specific example.
examples: I enjoy outdoor sports, in particular hiking.
The report highlights one issue in particular: cost.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which sports do you enjoy most?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I enjoy outdoor sports, in particular hiking.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: In comparison, the smaller model uses less energy.
The first test was simple; in comparison, the second was difficult.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which model uses less energy?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In comparison, the smaller model uses less energy.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: The hotel is expensive but comfortable in other respects.
The new plan is slower but better in other respects.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is the hotel worth the price?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The hotel is expensive but comfortable in other respects.

cards.usageNote: Shows how another example or argument follows a similar pattern.
examples: We tested the first device; the second was tested in the same way.
She supports new staff in the same way she was supported.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Were both devices tested differently?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: We tested the first device; the second was tested in the same way.

cards.usageNote: Adds a concrete illustration or highlights a specific example.
examples: The report assessed the overall budget; more specifically, it examined maintenance costs.
We need better data; more specifically, we need prices from rural areas.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which costs did the report examine?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The report assessed the overall budget; more specifically, it examined maintenance costs.

cards.usageNote: Places actions or ideas in a clear time or presentation order.
examples: I prepared dinner; meanwhile, she set the table.
The city grew; meanwhile, the nearby villages shrank.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What was she doing while you cooked?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I prepared dinner; meanwhile, she set the table.

cards.usageNote: Introduces a contrast or a result that remains true despite an obstacle.
examples: The path was steep; nevertheless, we reached the top.
The results were limited; nevertheless, the team continued.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Did you reach the top of the mountain?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The path was steep; nevertheless, we reached the top.

cards.usageNote: Links evidence or an action to its outcome, consequence or purpose.
examples: The cost rose; consequently, fewer people signed up.
The road closed; consequently, buses changed routes.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did fewer people register?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The cost rose; consequently, fewer people signed up.

cards.usageNote: Explains a reason, cause or justification for an action or conclusion.
examples: The data are incomplete; for this reason, we need another test.
She was ill; for this reason, the meeting moved online.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why do you need another test?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The data are incomplete; for this reason, we need another test.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: In response to complaints, the company changed its policy.
She smiled in response to the invitation.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did they change the policy?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In response to complaints, the company changed its policy.

cards.usageNote: Limits a claim or clarifies which aspect, exception or context matters.
examples: With regard to your request, we need more details.
The report raises questions with regard to safety.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What about my request?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: With regard to your request, we need more details.

cards.usageNote: Limits a claim or clarifies which aspect, exception or context matters.
examples: In terms of price, this laptop is a better deal.
The city has improved in terms of public transport.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which laptop is better value?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In terms of price, this laptop is a better deal.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: I'd prefer a quiet café as opposed to a crowded bar.
The study measures behavior as opposed to opinions.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What kind of place would you prefer?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I'd prefer a quiet café as opposed to a crowded bar.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: In the event of a fire, use the stairs.
In the event of delays, passengers will be notified.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What should we do if there's a fire?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In the event of a fire, use the stairs.

cards.usageNote: Compares differences between two choices, observations or claims.
examples: The first plan is expensive; by contrast, the second is affordable.
Older devices were bulky; by contrast, these are light.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Which plan costs less?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The first plan is expensive; by contrast, the second is affordable.

cards.usageNote: Places actions or ideas in a clear time or presentation order.
examples: To begin with, let's review the main problem.
To begin with, we need a clear budget.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Where should we start?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: To begin with, let's review the main problem.

cards.usageNote: Summarizes a practical conclusion without repeating every detail.
examples: To sum up, the changes saved time and money.
To sum up, both options have risks.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What's your overall conclusion?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: To sum up, the changes saved time and money.

cards.usageNote: Summarizes a practical conclusion without repeating every detail.
examples: In short, the plan needs more time.
In short, we couldn't reach an agreement.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: How did the meeting go?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In short, the plan needs more time.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: The new system may save money in the long run.
Regular practice pays off in the long run.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is the new system worth the cost?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: The new system may save money in the long run.

cards.usageNote: Links ideas logically in spoken or written English; read both examples to notice the relationship.
examples: In the short term, repairs will slow traffic.
The changes may be difficult in the short term.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Will the repairs affect traffic now?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In the short term, repairs will slow traffic.

cards.usageNote: Explains a reason, cause or justification for an action or conclusion.
examples: In light of the new evidence, we changed the plan.
In light of recent events, the meeting was postponed.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Why did you change the plan?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: In light of the new evidence, we changed the plan.

cards.usageNote: Explains a reason, cause or justification for an action or conclusion.
examples: Given that it's late, let's continue tomorrow.
Given that costs are rising, we should review the budget.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Should we keep working tonight?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Given that it's late, let's continue tomorrow.

cards.usageNote: Sets a condition, limit or possible situation affecting the main statement.
examples: You can join on the condition that you follow the rules.
We'll proceed on the condition that everyone agrees.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Can anyone join the group?

dialogue.speaker: B
